subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 10! In this unit you become a data detective. Data is just a special word for information that we gather to answer a question or to help us make a good decision. Every day, all around you, people collect data. When Amina counts how many goats come home to the pen each evening, when a shopkeeper in the Hargeisa market keeps track of which fruit sells the fastest, and when a football coach writes down how many goals each player scores, they are all collecting and recording data.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 4 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: This unit is designed for self-paced learning. That means you move at your own speed. Read each explanation slowly, try every worked example yourself on paper, and only move on when you feel ready. Your AI tutor is available day and night to give you extra practice, explain a step in a new way, invent fresh questions, or check your answers. Your teacher will also meet with you about twice a week to help with anything that feels tricky.

Why do these skills matter so much? Because data helps us understand the world and make fair, sensible choices. Scientists collect data when they do experiments. Nurses at a clinic in Mogadishu record how many children come for check-ups. Business people collect data about what customers like so they do not waste money making things nobody wants. When Sofia wants to bake cakes for the school fair, she does not guess which flavour to make. She *collects data* by asking people what they like, and then she decides. Good data leads to good decisions.

As you work, keep a pencil, a ruler, and some squared paper beside you. Mathematics is not a subject you can learn only by reading. You must do it. Draw the tally marks, build the tables, plot the dots, and say your conclusions out loud. If you make a mistake, that is not a failure. It is simply a signal that shows you exactly what to practise next. Let us begin our data adventure!
Tell the difference between a statistical question and a question with only one answer.
Plan an investigation: choose a question, decide what data to collect, and plan how to record it.
Collect and record data systematically so it is accurate and easy to read.
Create and read a tally chart, using tally marks correctly in groups of five.
Turn tally marks into a frequency table and use it to answer questions.
Create and interpret a dot plot above a labelled number line.
Draw conclusions from a data display, such as the most common value or the range.

concepts.title: What Is Data and What Is a Statistical Question?
concepts.explanation:
Data is information we collect to help us answer a question or make a decision. Data comes in different shapes. Sometimes it is numbers, like how many children are in a class. Sometimes it is categories, like favourite colours or types of pets. Sometimes it is measurements, like the heights of plants in a garden or the temperature each day. Whatever form it takes, data is only useful when we collect it carefully and record it clearly.

Not every question is worth collecting data for. A statistical question is a special kind of question. It is one that we answer by collecting data, and one where we expect the answers to be different from person to person or from thing to thing. That variety is the whole point.

Compare these two questions. 'How many books do the children in our class read each month?' is a statistical question, because different children will read different numbers of books, so we must collect data to answer it. But 'What is 5 + 7?' is not a statistical question, because there is only one correct answer, which is 12. We do not need to survey anybody to find it. Learning to tell these two kinds of question apart is the first skill of a data detective.
concepts.example: Here are some more statistical questions to help the idea settle in your mind: How many pets do people in our street have? What are the favourite fruits of the children at Nuur Academy? How many star jumps can each learner do in one minute? How tall are the young mango trees in the school garden? Each of these needs data, and each will give a *spread* of different answers. Now here are questions that are not statistical: What is the capital of Kenya? How many days are in a week? What is 10 multiplied by 5? Each of those has a single fixed answer, so there is nothing to investigate.

concepts.title: Planning an Investigation
concepts.explanation:
Once you have a good statistical question, you cannot just rush out and start counting. You need a plan. Planning an investigation means thinking ahead so that the data you collect is accurate, fair, and useful. A good plan follows these clear steps:

Choose your question. Make sure it is clear and that it can truly be answered with data.

Decide what data to collect. Think about exactly what information will help answer your question.

Plan how to collect the data. Will you count, measure, or ask people a question?

Choose how to record the data. Will you use a table, a tally chart, a dot plot, or another method?

Collect and record your data. Be careful and accurate; do not miss anyone out and do not count anyone twice.

Look at your data and answer your question. What does the data actually tell you?

Let us watch a real plan in action. Aisha wants to answer the question 'How many star jumps can we do in one minute?' She decides to use four friends from her class. She will ask each friend to do star jumps for exactly one minute while she counts. The equipment she needs is a stopwatch, some paper, and a pencil. She will record the results in a simple table with each name and each number.

Here are the results Aisha collected:

Now Aisha looks at her data and answers her question. Eli did the most star jumps, with 32. Cerys did the least, with 24. The total for the four friends was 30 + 24 + 27 + 32 = 113 star jumps. Notice how the careful plan led straight to clear answers. That is exactly what good planning does for you.
concepts.example: When you plan your own investigation, the same four sentences help every time. Copy and complete them: 'The people I will use are ___. I will ask the people to ___. The equipment I will need is ___. I will record the data using ___.' If you can finish those four sentences sensibly, your plan is ready.

concepts.title: Tally Charts
concepts.explanation:
A tally chart is one of the best tools for collecting data while it is happening. A tally chart records data by making small marks, called tally marks, to count items in different categories. Tally marks are simply straight vertical lines. The clever part is how we group them: after every four marks, the fifth mark is drawn as a line straight across the previous four. This makes the marks into neat bundles of five, which are very fast to count.

For example, to record the number 7, you draw a group of five (four lines with the fifth across them) and then two more single lines, which we can write as IIII II. To record 3, you simply draw III. Grouping in fives means you never have to count a long row of single lines one at a time. You count the fives, then add on the leftovers.

Here is how to create a tally chart, step by step:

Decide what categories you need (for example, each shoe size, or each favourite fruit).

Draw a table with a column for the categories and a column for the tallies.

For each item you count, add one tally mark in the correct category.

After every four marks in a category, draw the fifth mark across the other four.

When you have finished, count the tally marks in each category to find the frequency.

Let us build a tally chart from real data. These are the shoe sizes of the children in Class 4, written down as they were called out: 34, 30, 32, 34, 34, 31, 33, 36, 36, 34, 32, 35, 36, 37, 34, 31, 35, 34, 33, 35. As we go through the list, we place a tally mark next to the matching size. When we are done and count the marks, we get this tally chart and frequency table:

Now we can read the chart and learn things. Size 34 is the most common shoe size in the class, worn by 6 children. Sizes 30 and 37 are the least common, worn by just 1 child each. If we add up all the frequencies (1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 6 + 3 + 3 + 1) we get 20 children altogether. Reading a tally chart is like listening to what the data is quietly telling you.
concepts.example: When are tally charts especially useful? They shine when you are collecting data in real time, like counting cars passing the masjid, or votes as they are called out. They work beautifully for sorting items into categories. They make it easy to count a large number of items without losing your place. And they always show the exact count for each category. Whenever you need to keep a running count as things happen, reach for a tally chart.

concepts.title: Frequency Tables
concepts.explanation:
A frequency table is very close cousin to a tally chart. The word frequency simply means *how many times* something happens or appears. When you count up the tally marks in each category and write down the number, you have made a frequency table. In fact, most tally charts have a frequency column right beside the tallies, so you can see both at once, just like the shoe-size chart above.

Why bother turning tallies into numbers? Because numbers are quicker to compare and easier to calculate with. Once the shoe-size data is written as frequencies (1, 2, 2, 2, 6, 3, 3, 1), we can quickly find the total by adding, or find how many more children wear size 34 than size 35 by subtracting: 6 − 3 = 3 more children. The tally marks help us *collect* accurately; the frequency numbers help us *think* clearly.
concepts.example: Here is a small worked idea. Suppose a tally chart of favourite fruits shows Apple IIII III, Banana IIII I, Orange IIII, Strawberry IIII II, and Grapes IIII. Reading each group of five plus its leftovers gives the frequency table: Apple 8, Banana 6, Orange 4, Strawberry 7, Grapes 5. Now, without recounting any marks, we can say the total number of children asked was 8 + 6 + 4 + 7 + 5 = 30 children, and that apple was the most popular fruit. The frequency numbers did the heavy lifting.

concepts.title: Dot Plots
concepts.explanation:
A dot plot is another clear way to display data, and it is especially good for numbers. In a dot plot, we draw a horizontal number line, and above each number we place one dot for every time that number appears in the data. If a value appears many times, the dots stack up on top of one another, making a little tower. The taller the tower, the more often that value happens.

Here is how to create a dot plot, step by step:

Draw a horizontal number line that is long enough to show every value in your data.

Label the number line so everyone knows what the numbers mean.

For each value in your data, place one dot above that number on the line.

If a value appears more than once, stack the dots neatly, one above the other.

It is best to use squared paper so your dots line up and are evenly spaced. Even spacing matters, because a dot plot tells its story through its *shape*, and a messy plot hides the shape.

Let us make one. Here is data about how many pets each learner has: 0, 1, 3, 1, 1, 0, 2, 4, 1, 2, 2, 0, 0, 1, 3, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0. First we count how many times each value appears: 0 pets appears 6 times, 1 pet appears 6 times, 2 pets appears 5 times, 3 pets appears 2 times, and 4 pets appears 1 time. We then draw six dots above 0, six dots above 1, five dots above 2, two dots above 3, and one dot above 4. The dot plot would look like this (each dot drawn as a small circle):

above 0: o o o o o o above 1: o o o o o o above 2: o o o o o above 3: o o above 4: o

Reading the finished plot tells us a lot. Most learners have 0 or 1 pet, because those towers are the tallest. No learner has 5 pets, because there is no dot above 5. Only one learner has 4 pets. And the number of pets ranges from 0 to 4. Notice how quickly the *shape* of the plot shows us where the data bunches up.
concepts.example: Dot plots are especially useful when you want to see how data is spread out, when you want to compare different values easily, when your data set is not too large, and when the data is made of whole numbers in a limited range (like 0 to 5). They give you a picture you can read at a glance.

concepts.title: Reading Information from a Dot Plot
concepts.explanation:
Making a dot plot is only half the skill. The other half is reading one that somebody else has drawn. To read a dot plot, first look at the label on the number line so you understand what the numbers mean. Then count the dots above each number to find how many times that value appears. Then look for patterns, such as which value has the tallest tower. Finally, compare different values to see how the data is spread.

Here is a dot plot showing how many hours of sport each learner does each week. Counting the towers gives us: 1 dot above 0, 2 dots above 1, 3 dots above 2, 3 dots above 3, 2 dots above 4, no dots above 5, 1 dot above 6, none above 7, and none above 8.
concepts.example: From this plot we can answer many questions. 1 learner does 0 hours of sport. 3 learners do exactly 2 hours. No learner does 5 or 7 hours. And here is a harder one: how many learners do more than 2 hours of sport each week? We must add up every tower to the right of 2: the 3 learners at 3 hours, plus 2 learners at 4 hours, plus 1 learner at 6 hours. That gives 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 learners who do more than 2 hours of sport. Always read the label and count carefully, and the dot plot will answer almost anything you ask it.

methods.title: How to plan an investigation
methods.example: Work through these with me. Cover the solution, try it yourself first, then check every step.
steps: Choose a clear statistical question.
Decide what data to collect and who to ask.
Plan how to collect it: count, measure, or ask.
Choose how to record it: table, tally chart, or dot plot.
Collect carefully, then read the data to answer your question.

methods.title: How to make a tally chart and frequency table
methods.example: Write the number 7 correctly using tally marks.
steps: List the categories in a table.
Add one tally mark per item, grouping in fives.
Count the tally marks in each row.
Write that count as the frequency number.

methods.title: How to read a dot plot
methods.example: A pet tally chart shows: Dog IIII II (7), Cat IIII (5), Fish III (3), Rabbit II (2), Hamster IIII (4), Bird I (1). How many children were surveyed in total, and how many more have dogs than rabbits?
steps: Read the label on the number line.
Count the dots in each tower.
Find the tallest tower for the most common value.
For 'more than', add all the towers to the right of the value.

methods.title: Build a tally chart
methods.example: Make a tally-and-frequency chart for this data about favourite fruit: Apple 8, Banana 6, Orange 4, Strawberry 7, Grapes 5.
steps: Solution: Turn each number into groups of five plus leftovers.
Apple 8 = IIII III; Banana 6 = IIII I; Orange 4 = IIII; Strawberry 7 = IIII II; Grapes 5 = IIII.
The frequencies stay 8, 6, 4, 7, 5, and the total is 8 + 6 + 4 + 7 + 5 = 30 children.

methods.title: Make a dot plot
methods.example: Show this data on a dot plot: number of books read = 2, 3, 0, 1, 4, 2, 3, 5, 2, 1, 3, 4, 0, 2, 3, 1, 2, 5, 3, 2.
steps: Solution: First count each value.
0 appears 2 times, 1 appears 3 times, 2 appears 6 times, 3 appears 5 times, 4 appears 2 times, 5 appears 2 times.
Draw a number line labelled 'Number of books read' from 0 to 5, then stack that many dots above each number.
The tallest tower is above 2, so 2 books is the most common.

methods.title: Read a dot plot (siblings)
methods.example: A dot plot of siblings has these towers: 1 sibling has 2 dots, 2 siblings have 4 dots, 3 siblings have 3 dots, 4 siblings have 2 dots, 6 siblings has 1 dot. How many children were surveyed, and what is the range?
steps: Solution: Add every dot: 2 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 12 children.
The range is from the lowest value to the highest value, which is from 1 sibling to 6 siblings.
Notice there are no dots above 5, so nobody had exactly 5 siblings, but 6 is still the highest value present.

workedExamples.title: Is it a statistical question?
workedExamples.prompt: Work through these with me. Cover the solution, try it yourself first, then check every step.
workedExamples.solution: Worked Example 1: Is it a statistical question? Decide whether each is a statistical question: (a) How many siblings do the children in our class have? (b) What is the capital of Uganda? Solution: (a) is a statistical question, because different children have different numbers of siblings, so we must collect data. (b) is not a statistical question, because there is only one correct answer (Kampala), which we do not need to survey. The test is always: do we expect different answers, and must we collect data?

workedExamples.title: Show 7 in tally marks
workedExamples.prompt: Write the number 7 correctly using tally marks.
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Group in fives. First draw a bundle of five (four lines with the fifth across them), then add two more single lines. So 7 is written IIII II (a five-group plus two). It is *not* correct to write seven separate single lines, because grouping in fives is what makes tally marks fast to count.

workedExamples.title: Read a tally chart
workedExamples.prompt: A pet tally chart shows: Dog IIII II (7), Cat IIII (5), Fish III (3), Rabbit II (2), Hamster IIII (4), Bird I (1). How many children were surveyed in total, and how many more have dogs than rabbits?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Add all the frequencies: 7 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 4 + 1 = 22 children in total. For the second part, subtract: dogs minus rabbits is 7 − 2 = 5 more children have dogs than rabbits. The frequency numbers made both answers quick.

workedExamples.title: Build a tally chart
workedExamples.prompt: Make a tally-and-frequency chart for this data about favourite fruit: Apple 8, Banana 6, Orange 4, Strawberry 7, Grapes 5.
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Turn each number into groups of five plus leftovers. Apple 8 = IIII III; Banana 6 = IIII I; Orange 4 = IIII; Strawberry 7 = IIII II; Grapes 5 = IIII. The frequencies stay 8, 6, 4, 7, 5, and the total is 8 + 6 + 4 + 7 + 5 = 30 children.

workedExamples.title: Make a dot plot
workedExamples.prompt: Show this data on a dot plot: number of books read = 2, 3, 0, 1, 4, 2, 3, 5, 2, 1, 3, 4, 0, 2, 3, 1, 2, 5, 3, 2.
workedExamples.solution: Solution: First count each value. 0 appears 2 times, 1 appears 3 times, 2 appears 6 times, 3 appears 5 times, 4 appears 2 times, 5 appears 2 times. Draw a number line labelled 'Number of books read' from 0 to 5, then stack that many dots above each number. The tallest tower is above 2, so 2 books is the most common. Always count the values before you draw.

workedExamples.title: Read a dot plot (siblings)
workedExamples.prompt: A dot plot of siblings has these towers: 1 sibling has 2 dots, 2 siblings have 4 dots, 3 siblings have 3 dots, 4 siblings have 2 dots, 6 siblings has 1 dot. How many children were surveyed, and what is the range?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Add every dot: 2 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 12 children. The range is from the lowest value to the highest value, which is from 1 sibling to 6 siblings. Notice there are no dots above 5, so nobody had exactly 5 siblings, but 6 is still the highest value present.

workedExamples.title: Choose the right method
workedExamples.prompt: Would you use a tally chart, a dot plot, or both for: (a) the eye colours of your class, (b) the number of goals scored in football matches?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: (a) Eye colours are categories, not numbers, so a tally chart is best. (b) Goals scored are numbers, so you could use a tally chart to collect them and a dot plot to show the spread, so both are appropriate. Always ask first: is my data categories or numbers?

workedExamples.title: Compare two data sets
workedExamples.prompt: Class A read (using value × frequency): 0×2, 1×3, 2×4, 3×3, 4×2, 5×1 books. Class B read: 0×1, 1×2, 2×3, 3×5, 4×3, 5×1. Which class read more in total?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Class A total = 0 + 3 + 8 + 9 + 8 + 5 = 33 books. Class B total = 0 + 2 + 6 + 15 + 12 + 5 = 40 books. Since 40 is greater than 33, Class B read more books in total. Multiplying each value by its frequency, then adding, is the fair way to compare.

workedExamples.title: How many more children chose water than tea
workedExamples.prompt: How many more children chose water than tea?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: The frequencies are Water 8, Milk 5, Juice 7, Tea 3. Subtract to compare: 8 − 3 = 5, so 5 more children chose water than tea.

workedExamples.title: Practice 10
workedExamples.prompt: Turn this data into a frequency table for number of goals: 1, 0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1. Which number of goals is most common?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Count each value in the list 1, 0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1. The frequencies are: 0 appears 2 times, 1 appears 4 times, 2 appears 3 times, 3 appears 1 time. Since 1 has the highest frequency, 1 goal is the most common.

workedExamples.title: Practice 11
workedExamples.prompt: A dot plot of test scores has towers: 7 has 5 dots, 8 has 4 dots, 9 has 3 dots, 10 has 3 dots. How many children took the test?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Add every tower: 5 + 4 + 3 + 3 = 15 children took the test.

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: For that same score plot, how many children scored more than 8?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: 'More than 8' means the towers above 9 and 10: 3 + 3 = 6 children scored more than 8.

activities.title: Family Favourites Survey
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and your family or neighbours.
steps: Choose a statistical question, such as 'What is your favourite fruit?' (mango, banana, papaya, dates, orange).
Draw a tally chart with a row for each fruit.
Ask at least ten people and add one tally mark for each answer, grouping in fives.
Count the tallies to make a frequency table, then write one sentence about the most popular fruit.
Keep your chart. You have just carried out a real investigation from question to conclusion!

activities.title: The One-Minute Challenge
activities.materials: a stopwatch or clock, paper, a pencil, and a few friends or family members.
steps: Pick a fair challenge, such as 'How many star jumps can we do in one minute?'
Time each person for exactly one minute while you count carefully.
Record each name and number in a table, just like Aisha did in the lesson.
Find the greatest, the least, and the total. Who did the most? What was the total?

activities.title: Tally the Traffic (Investigation)
activities.materials: a safe place to sit and watch a road, paper, and a pencil.
steps: Draw a tally chart with rows for cars, buses, bicycles, and people walking.
For ten minutes, add a tally mark each time one goes past, grouping in fives.
Turn your tallies into a frequency table. Which was the most common? Which was the least?
Do it again at a different time of day and compare. Was there more traffic near a prayer time?

activities.title: Dot Plot of the Week
steps: Each day for a week, count something that changes, such as cups of camel milk drunk, or minutes of reading.
Write down the seven numbers you collect.
Draw a labelled number line and place one dot above each value, stacking repeats.
Read your dot plot: what value happened most often, and what is the range?

activities.title: Tally vs Dot Plot Game (Family or Group)
activities.materials: number cards or a small pile of counting objects, and two players.
steps: Collect a set of numbers, for example how many siblings each person in the room has.
Player 1 records the data as a tally-and-frequency chart. Player 2 records the same data as a dot plot.
Compare the two displays. Which was faster to make? Which shows the spread more clearly?
Talk about when you would choose each method in real life.

activities.title: Which Book Is Easier to Read? (Investigation)
activities.materials: two storybooks and a page of paper.
steps: Choose one page from each book. Decide what data shows a book is easier to read (for example, the number of short words, or words with fewer than five letters).
Count and tally your chosen data on each page.
Display the data in a small table so the two books sit side by side.
Write two sentences: what is the same about the books, and what is different?

After your activities, talk or write about these questions: Which activity helped you understand tally charts and dot plots best? What was the trickiest part of collecting data fairly? Did you ever miss someone out or count twice, and how did you fix it? What would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session, or with your AI tutor right away.

rules.title: Statistical Question Rule
rules.text: A statistical question is answered by collecting data. It has different answers, not one fixed answer. How many pets do people have? is statistical. What is 5 + 7? is not.

rules.title: Tally Mark Rule
rules.text: Draw straight lines and group them in fives. The fifth mark goes across the other four. So a five-group plus two extra lines means 7.

rules.title: Dot Plot Rule
rules.text: Draw and label a number line. Place one dot above a value for each time it appears. Stack repeated dots and keep them evenly spaced.

terms: Information collected to answer a question

How many times a value appears
A table of categories and their counts
Dots above a number line showing data
How the data is spread out
From the lowest value to the highest value
commonMistakes: Ask: do we expect different answers?
Tally marks in a long row
Group in fives, fifth mark across
Line dots up on squared paper
Always label and title the display
Tally for categories, dot plot for numbers

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A tally chart is better for categories (words) such as favourite sport, because it sorts groups and gives exact counts; a dot plot is better for numbers in a small range such as number of pets, because it shows the spread.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: More than 2 hours means towers above 3, 4 and 6: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 learners.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Dot Plots.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A dot plot is another clear way to display data, and it is especially good for numbers. In a dot plot, we draw a horizontal number line, and above each number we place one dot for every time that number appears in the data. If a value appears many times, the dots stack up on top of one another, making a little tower. The taller the tower, the more often that value happens. reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Reading Information from a Dot Plot.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Making a dot plot is only half the skill. The other half is reading one that somebody else has drawn. To read a dot plot, first look at the label on the number line so you understand what the numbers mean. Then count the dots above each number to find how many times that value appears. Then look for patterns, such as which value has the tallest tower. Finally, compare different values to see how the data is spread.

Here is a dot plot showing how many hours of sport each learner does each week. Counting the towers gives us: 1 dot above 0, 2 dots above 1, 3 dots above 2, 3 dots above 3, 2 dots above 4, no dots above 5, 1 dot above 6, none above 7, and none above 8.

questions.question: Which of these is a statistical question?
options: How many pets does each child in the class have?
What is 6 + 5?
What is the capital of Somalia?
How many days are in a week?
questions.answer: How many pets does each child in the class have?
questions.hint: A statistical question expects different answers from different people, so we must collect data.
questions.explanation: Different children have different numbers of pets, so we must collect data to answer this question. The other questions each have one fixed answer, so they are not statistical questions.

questions.question: Hodan wants to find out her classmates' favourite fruit. What should she do first when planning her investigation?
options: Choose a clear question, such as 'What is your favourite fruit?'
Guess the answer without asking anyone
Draw the frequency table before asking any questions
Only ask her best friend and stop there
questions.answer: Choose a clear question, such as 'What is your favourite fruit?'
questions.hint: Planning an investigation always starts with a clear question.
questions.explanation: The first step of planning an investigation is to choose a clear statistical question, before deciding what data to collect and how to record it.

questions.question: Which of these is the best way to collect and record data systematically?
options: Use a tally chart and add one mark for each item, grouping in fives
Try to remember the count in your head until the end
Write down only the final total, with no record of each item
Guess the total after watching for one minute
questions.answer: Use a tally chart and add one mark for each item, grouping in fives
questions.hint: Systematic recording means keeping an accurate mark for every single item as it happens.
questions.explanation: A tally chart lets you record data accurately as it happens, adding one mark per item and grouping in fives, so nothing is missed or double counted.

questions.explanation: 8 is a five-group (IIII) plus three more single lines, written as IIII III.

The range of the data is 2

questions.hint: The tallest tower on a dot plot shows the value that happens most often.
